{{Short description|Series of radiocarbon dating tests performed on the Dead Sea Scrolls}}
'''Carbon dating the Dead Sea Scrolls''' refers to a series of [[radiocarbon dating]] tests performed on the [[Dead Sea Scrolls]], first by the AMS ([[Accelerator Mass Spectrometry]]) lab of the [[ETH Zurich|Zurich Institute of Technology]] in 1991 and then by the AMS Facility at the [[University of Arizona]] in Tucson in 1994–95. There was also a historical test of a piece of linen performed in 1946 by [[Willard Libby]], the inventor of the dating method.

==Testing==
One of the earliest carbon dating tests was carried out on November 14, 1950. This was on a piece of linen from Qumran Cave 1, the resulting date range being 167&nbsp;BCE – 233&nbsp;CE.<ref>{{Cite book|author1=VanderKam, James C. |author2=Flint, Peter |title=The Meaning of the Dead Sea Scrolls|publisher=HarperSanFrancisco|location=New York|date=2002|page=27}}</ref> Libby had first started using the dating method in 1946 and the early testing required relatively large samples, so testing on scrolls themselves only became feasible when methods used in the dating process were improved upon.<ref>Doudna, G. "Carbon-14 Dating", in ''Encyclopedia of the Dead Sea Scrolls'', Schiffman, Lawrence, & VanderKam, James, eds., Vol.1 (Oxford: 2000)</ref> [[F. E. Zeuner|F.E. Zeuner]] carried out tests on date palm wood from the Qumran site yielding a date range of 70&nbsp;BCE – 90&nbsp;CE.<ref>{{Cite book|author1=VanderKam, James C. |author2=Flint, Peter |title=The Meaning of the Dead Sea Scrolls|publisher=HarperSanFrancisco|location=New York|date=2002|page=28}}</ref> In 1963 Libby tested a sample from the Isaiah Scroll, which provided a range of 200&nbsp;BCE – 1&nbsp;CE.<ref>Carmi, Israel, "Radiocarbon Dating of the Dead Sea Scrolls" in ''The Dead Sea Scrolls: Fifty Years after their Discovery. 1947–1997'', Schiffman, Lawrence, Tov, Emanuel, & VanderKam, James, eds., (Jerusalem: IES, 2000) p. 881.</ref>

In 1991, [[Robert Eisenman]] and [[Philip R. Davies]] made a demand to date a number of scrolls, which led to a series of tests carried out in Zurich on samples from fourteen scrolls. Among these were samples from other sites around the Dead Sea, which contained date indications within the text to supply a control for the carbon dating results.<ref name="vkf">{{Cite book|author1=VanderKam, James C. |author2=Flint, Peter |title=The Meaning of the Dead Sea Scrolls|publisher=HarperSanFrancisco|location=New York|date=2002|pages=28–29}}</ref> A similar battery of tests was carried out in 1994–95 in Tucson, this time with samples from twenty-two scrolls as well as another piece of linen.<ref name="vkf"/>

In 2025, a series of radiocarbon tests were carried out on samples from thirty scrolls. The samples were distributed as 25 from the [[Qumran Caves]], 1 from [[Masada]], 2 from the [[Murabbaat]] caves, and 2 from the [[Nahal Hever]] caves. The study also made use of an [[AI]]-based date-prediction model called "Enoch", which was trained by applying [[Bayesian ridge regression]] on the handwriting-style descriptors of 24 of the 14C-dated samples, for the [[Palaeography|paleographic dating]] of some 135 previously undated manuscripts.<ref>{{Cite journal |title=Dating ancient manuscripts using radiocarbon and AI-based writing style analysis |journal=PLOS ONE |last=Popović |first=Mladen |volume=20 |issue=6 |article-number=e0323185 |last2=Dhali |first2=Maruf A. |last3=Schomaker |first3=Lambert |last4=Plicht |first4=Johannes van der |last5=Rasmussen |first5=Kaare Lund |last6=Nasa |first6=Jacopo La |last7=Degano |first7=Ilaria |last8=Colombini |first8=Maria Perla |last9=Tigchelaar |first9=Eibert |year=2025 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0323185 |issn=1932-6203 |pmc=12136314 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

==14C Test results==
The following table shows all the [[Qumran]]-related samples that were tested by Zurich ('''Z'''), Tucson ('''T''') and Libby ('''L'''). The column headed "14C Age" provides a raw age before 1950 for each sample tested. This represents the ideal date for the amount of 14C measured for the sample. However, as the quantity of 14 absorbed by all life fluctuates from year to year, the figure must be calibrated based on known fluctuation. This calibrated range of dates is represented in the last column, given with a '''2-sigma''' error rating, which means at 95% confidence. With the exception of the first text from Wadi-ed-Daliyeh, the texts in the table below are only those from the caves around Qumran. The table orders them chronologically, based on 14C age.

Many of the date ranges provided are actually two date ranges, for example the Habakkuk Commentary (#13), which is given as 160–148 or 111–2&nbsp;CE. The section of the calibration curve for the 14C age of the Habakkuk Commentary is complex, so that the 14C age of 2054 cuts through a few spikes on the curve, providing two date ranges.

==Observations==
The Great Isaiah Scroll 1QIsa<sup>a</sup> has been tested three times, once by Libby, once at Zurich and once at Tucson. The results from the latter two were almost identical, which is a good indicator of the basic accuracy of this dating method. 1QS (#15), tested at Zurich, and 4QSam<sup>c</sup> (#8), tested at Tucson, provide overlapping date ranges, which is expected when both texts are attributed to the same scribe.<ref>Doudna 1998, p. 450.</ref> When 4Q258 (#24) was tested at Tucson its result was so anomalous (129–255 or 303–318&nbsp;CE) that the laboratory was asked to retest another sample from the same document. The second test (#21) yielded a result (50&nbsp;BCE–130&nbsp;CE) that was deemed more satisfactory.
